paper_title: Reflex: Visually Grounded Reactive Humanoid Control

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Humans effortlessly react to the world; they adeptly return a tennis shot, catch a falling cup, step aside from a passing cart, or pass a box tossed during truck unloading. These everyday actions require anticipating a moving target and reflexively responding with the whole body within about a second. Such visual reactive whole-body control remains challenging for humanoids, which must (1) coordinate whole-body control, (2) react to object dynamics in real time, and (3) ground perception in egocentric vision. We study catching thrown boxes as a representative task that demands all three capabilities; existing systems cover only part of it, relying on end-effectors, motion capture, or marked objects. We present Reflex, a three-stage framework that learns these capabilities stage by stage while connecting them through a compact representation of object dynamics. First, a state-based policy learns whole-body catching with reinforcement learning. Second, the policy learns to infer the dynamics of a moving box from delayed and incomplete observations. Third, an egocentric RGB-D encoder learns to recover this dynamics representation directly from visual observations while keeping the whole-body controller fixed. This decomposition provides each capability with a direct training signal and makes visual learning substantially more scalable. In simulation, Reflex achieves 85.7% catch success from egocentric RGB-D, compared with 87.9% when given privileged box observations. Temporal visual history is critical: removing it reduces success by 35.6 and 39.8 points on centered and laterally offset throws. On a real Unitree G1, Reflex catches human-thrown boxes with 65% and 40% success at 2.5 and 5 m, reaching 76% and 59% of human catchers' success at the same distances.

sections.content: Reflex: Visually Grounded Reactive Humanoid Control Taoyang Jia1,2, Weikai Huang1, Linxin Song3, Jared Darlington1, Jieyu Zhao3, Yue Wang3, Jiafei Duan4, Zhongzheng Ren5,6, and Ranjay Krishna1 3University of Southern California 1University of Washington 2Stanford University 4National University of Singapore 5University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill 6Allen Institute for AI Fig. 1. Visual reactive whole-body catching on humanoid. (a) Catching thrown carton from onboard RGB-D input. (b)(d) Downstream application: carrying the box 7.8 m, handing it to person, and walking 7.3 back. The retained box is passed directly to the downstream walking controller for carrying and handover. to the world; Abstract Humans effortlessly react they adeptly return tennis shot, catch falling cup, step aside from passing cart, or pass box tossed during truck unloading. First, state-based policy learns wholebody catching with reinforcement learning. Second, the policy learns to infer the dynamics of moving box from delayed and incomplete observations. Third, an egocentric RGB-D encoder learns to recover this dynamics representation directly from visual observations while keeping the whole-body controller fixed. Equal contribution (co-first authors). I. INTRODUCTION Humans routinely react to fast-moving objects with their entire body. goalkeeper shifts, dives, and braces for an incoming shot; worker catches box tossed from truck; person reaches for falling cup while stepping to keep balance; another twists aside as cart passes unexpectedly close. These behaviors require more than tracking an object in motion. They require predicting where it will go, deciding how the body should meet or avoid it, and coordinating whole-body response before contact, often within about second. Humanoids have the morphology to perform such behaviors, but robust visually reactive whole-body control remains largely out of reach. This capability couples three challenges. First, the robot must control the whole body: it must place its feet and torso, move its arms into position, absorb impact, and remain balanced. Second, it must reflexively react to fast object dynamics under latency. In our real-robot trials, thrown box reaches the robot roughly one second after release, while camera-to-control latency alone has median of 69 ms in our detector-based pipeline. The robot therefore cannot simply react to the latest observation; it must infer where the object is going and commit to an interception before contact. Third, it must do so from egocentric vision. Because the camera moves with the robot, observed image motion combines object motion with self-motion, while the robots own arms increasingly occlude the object near contact. We study catching thrown boxes as representative test of all three challenges. Catching box is more demanding than intercepting ball with the hands: the robot must reposition its body, use the forearms and torso to form support, absorb the boxs momentum, and retain the load without losing balance. At the same time, the box is an ordinary uninstrumented object observed only through onboard RGBD cameras. The task is difficult even for people: across our trials, three human catchers succeed on only 28.3% of throws from 7 m. Existing systems address only parts of this problem. Robotic manipulators can catch moving objects from fixed or wheeled bases, avoiding the challenge of whole-body balance and impact absorption [1], [2], [3]. Recent humanoid systems demonstrate dynamic interactions such as punching away ball [4] or catching basketball with the hands [5], but rely on motion capture or retroreflective objects rather than grounding fast object motion from onboard vision. As result, whole-body control, fast prediction of object dynamics, and egocentric visual grounding have rarely been combined on real humanoid. We present Reflex, three-stage framework for visually reactive whole-body control (see Figure 2). Stage 1 learns whole-body catching from privileged simulator state using reinforcement learning and human motion priors. Stage 2 learns to infer the dynamics of moving box from delayed (2060 ms latency) and incomplete observations of its position, velocity, orientation, size, and observation age, producing latent representation that conditions the controller to react. Stage 3 learns to recover this same dynamics representation from egocentric RGB-D history and camera egomotion while keeping the whole-body controller fixed. Our decomposition gives each capability direct training signal and isolates expensive visual learning from reinforcement learning. In simulation, Reflex achieves 85.7% catch success from egocentric RGB-D, compared with 87.9% when given privileged box observations. Temporal visual history is vital for good performance; removing it reduces success by 35.6 and 39.8 points on centered and 0.6 m-offset throws. On real Unitree G1, Reflex catches human-thrown boxes on 65% and 40% of throws at 2.5 and 5 m, reaching 76% and 59% of the human success rate at the same distances (85.0% and 68.3%). Ablations further show that camera ego-motion matters for visual grounding, that regressing the learned latent works better than regressing the full privileged box state, and that action-matching initialization outperforms weight mapping by 5.2 points on average. More broadly, our results suggest path toward humanoids that can react to dynamic events directly from onboard vision, rather than relying on instrumented environments or task-specific perception systems. Catching is one instance of broader class of visually reactive whole-body skills, including interception, avoidance, handoffs, and physical assistance. These everyday tasks require predicting how the world will change and coordinating the body before contact. II. RELATED WORK We review prior work on catching thrown objects, on humanoid whole-body control and loco-manipulation, and on privileged learning for visual sim-to-real transfer. A. Catching thrown objects Catching thrown object requires predicting its trajectory and moving into position within short time window. Early systems addressed this with fixed-base arms guided by vision [6], with later work learning object dynamics and catching motions from demonstration [1] or planning impact-aware bimanual motions with fixed-base arms [7]. Learning-based approaches have since extended catching to whole-body model predictive control combined with policy learning [2], dexterous and bimanual throw-and-catch [8], [9], and mobile manipulators [10], [3]. More recently, bipedal humanoids have been trained to intercept balls as goalkeepers [4] and to catch basketball passes [5]. However, most of these systems observe the object with motion capture or fixed external cameras, with fewer relying on onboard sensing: humanoids have kicked and struck moving balls from onboard vision [11], [12], legged manipulator plays badminton with learned perception-error model [13], and onboard catching has been shown on wheeled humanoid [14] and quadruped [15], and concurrent work catches thrown box on humanoid from egocentric RGB without reporting realrobot success rates [16]. To address this, we train humanoid to catch and retain thrown box using onboard egocentric RGB-D. B. Humanoid whole-body control and loco-manipulation Human motion data has become common foundation for humanoid whole-body control. This approach began in physics-based character animation with motion imitation [17] and adversarial motion priors [18]. Extending interaction, Catch & Carry [19] paired this to object motor-primitive module learned from human demonstrations with an egocentric-vision policy trained by reinforcement learning to catch balls and carry boxes in simulation. These methods have since moved from simulation to hardware, where learned motion trackers provide general whole-body control on real humanoids [20], [21], [22]. Recent locomanipulation systems go further, lifting and carrying boxes and bulky objects through whole-body contact [23], [24], [25], [26], [27], [28]. In these tasks, though, the object is at rest when interaction begins, so the robot can approach and make contact at its own pace. Catching removes this freedom, since the body must already be in place when the box arrives. Like these methods, we build on human motion, but train dedicated catching controller that reacts to the incoming box and coordinates interception and retention. C. Privileged Learning and Visual Sim-to-Real Policies trained in simulation can use information that is unavailable at deployment, such as the exact state of an object. Privileged learning exploits this by training teacher with such information to supervise student Fig. 2. Training pipeline and policy architecture. Stage 1 learns whole-body control by training the state-policy teacher with PPO. Stage 2 learns the object dynamics: it initializes the privileged encoder and decoder latent-input weights by matching teacher actions, then jointly refines the encoder and decoder with PPO. Human motion examples supply reference tracking and an AMP style reward. Stage 3 learns visual grounding by predicting the latent from RGB-D histories and camera ego-motion, using box-state supervision and DAgger rollouts. The pretrained CNN and heatmap head stay fixed during GRU training; the privileged encoder and decoder remain fixed throughout Stage 3. The decoder also receives robot/reference observations. Because Stage 3 learns only the latent predictor, the visual controller reuses the PPO-trained decoder without modification. that uses onboard sensors [29], typically alongside asymmetric critics [30], domain randomization [31], and onpolicy data aggregation [32]. Legged robots adopted this approach early, with students that reproduce teachers latent from observation history [33], [34] or walk from egocentric depth [35]. Humanoids now use it to perform locomanipulation, door opening, parkour, and ladder climbing from depth or RGB [36], [37], [38], [39]. However, these students perceive static terrain or slow-moving objects. thrown box instead moves quickly through the view of moving camera. Following RMA [34], we keep the action decoder fixed and train visual model by latent regression to predict the privileged latent from RGB-D history and camera ego-motion. III. TASK FORMULATION At deployment, the visual input is stream of 192 144 RGB-D observations It from torso-mounted camera. The controller additionally receives the robot state required for whole-body stabilization, but no box pose, velocity, or external-camera measurement. The camera moves with the robot and the box becomes increasingly occluded near contact, making the task closed-loop coupling of visual estimation and whole-body response. At each 20 ms control step, the model outputs 29dimensional whole-body joint command, corresponding to one command for each actuated DoF. These commands are executed as joint-position targets. Thus, the task-level interface maps egocentric RGB-D observations and robot state directly to 29-DoF control; the internal policy decomposition is introduced only in Sec. IV. Simulation uses Isaac Lab [40], with physics at 200 Hz and control at 50 Hz.

sections.title: We first define the catching task and its sensing and control
sections.content: B. Success Criteria interface, then the criteria used to evaluate it. A. Visually Grounded Reactive Catching We study the task of catching human-thrown box with 29-degree-of-freedom (DoF) Unitree G1. The robot must move into the path of the incoming box, receive it on its forearms against the torso, dissipate its momentum, and retain it without falling. Unlike quasi-static loco-manipulation, the robot cannot choose when contact occurs: it must infer the box trajectory and coordinate its whole body before the box arrives. We evaluate three distinct outcomes. Interception indicates that the robot has arrested the incoming motion of the box: the box slows below 1 m/s near the torso, regardless of whether it is subsequently retained. The primary metric, catch success, additionally requires the box to be supported in the chest region, with the wrists on opposite sides of the box, without relying on the head or shoulders, and at low speed for 0.6 s. This criterion distinguishes sustained retention from incidental contact or momentary trap. We assess post-catch stability separately because retaining the box does not necessarily leave the robot in settled posture. Torso excursion records whether the torso tilt reaches 38 between launch and the end of the episode, while falls are reported independently. For the box-size sweep, where fixed chest-region test is not comparable across geometries, we use the geometry-agnostic sustained-hold criterion specified in Sec. V-A. These metrics separate perception and interception failures from retention and whole-body stabilization failures. IV. LEARNING EGOCENTRIC WHOLE-BODY CATCHING a) Perceptioncontrol decomposition: We decompose the deployed policy into visual perception function Vψ and whole-body control function πθ . Given history of egocentric RGB-D observations and camera ego-motion, Vψ predicts an eight-dimensional object-dynamics latent. The controller combines this latent with the robot/reference observation rt R160 and produces normalized 29-DoF action: (cid:98)zt = Vψ (ItK+1:t , etK+1:t ), at = πθ (rt ,(cid:98)zt ). (1) The action is converted to nominal joint-position targets as qnom = q0 + at , (2) where q0 R29 is the nominal joint configuration, R29 contains per-joint action scales, and denotes elementwise multiplication. This latent interface separates the question of what object information can be inferred from vision from how that information should drive the body. Training Vψ and πθ jointly from pixels with reinforcement learning is both computationally expensive and difficult to optimize. Every on-policy rollout would require highthroughput RGB-D rendering, while the policy must simultaneously explore large visual space and 29-dimensional action space. Catch success is delayed until contact and retention, providing weak supervision for learning object motion from images; camera ego-motion, intermittent occlusion, and policy-induced viewpoint changes further couple perception errors to the state distribution visited by the controller. monolithic end-to-end policy would therefore entangle visual representation learning with motor-skill discovery and make perception adaptation require retraining the controller. We instead organize learning into three stages, one per capability  (Fig. 2)  : Stage 1 learns whole-body control from box state with PPO, Stage 2 learns the object dynamics as compact control latent (its PPO also refines the controller), and Stage 3 grounds this latent in vision while the controller remains fixed. downstream carrying and handover module follows the catching controller (Sec. IV-D). A. Stage 1: Learning Whole-Body Control a) State observations and policy: We train statebased catching policy πstate with proximal policy optimization (PPO) [41] over successive warm-started runs. Its 170dimensional observation ostate combines the robot/reference input rt with ten box-state channels: pelvis-frame position and linear velocity (three each), observation age (one), and indicators of measurement jitter, freshness, and frozen observations (three). Simulation supplies these channels by corrupting box detections with randomized noise, missed observations, and delay and passing them through the Kalman filter used on hardware (gravity and linear drag). The actor is multilayer perceptron with hidden widths 512256128, exponential linear unit activations, and the 29 outputs of Eq. (2); an asymmetric critic additionally observes uncorrupted full-body poses and ground-truth box position and velocity. b) Catching objective and randomized training: Approach shaping encourages interception, hold shaping rewards forearm support near the chest, and sustainedcatch bonus rewards retention. Tracking retargeted human reference motion and an adversarial motion prior (AMP) [18] guide coordinated movement; penalties discourage excessive torso motion, abrupt commands, and falls. PPO updates the actor and critic, while the AMP discriminator learns from simulated motion and retargeted human examples. Throws, contact properties, and robot dynamics are randomized; held-box initializations and perturbations train retention and recovery. c) Teacher for latent transfer: After state-based PPO, we freeze the teacher. For Stage 2 action supervision, we query it with ground-truth position and velocity channels. Its decoder weights initialize the latent controller, and its actions label the initialization dataset. The ground-truth state-policy reference in the experiments instead feeds ideal (complete, noise-free, zero-delay) box measurements through the policys Kalman filter. B. This dataset aggregation (DAgger)- style procedure [32] expands DA with states encountered under latent control, and action matching is repeated on the aggregated data. These teacher action labels are distinct from the retargeted human motion examples used for reference tracking and the motion prior. d) Task-specific PPO refinement: After action matching and aggregation, PPO jointly optimizes the privileged encoder and the full decoder, using the catching objective and motion priors introduced in Stage 1. The asymmetric critic retains access to uncorrupted body poses and ground-truth box state while the actor receives rt and the dynamics latent computed from delayed box observations. Teacher action matching is used for initialization and aggregation; PPO refinement optimizes task return and, because the decoder is also updated, refines whole-body control as well (Sec. VC). Latent-controller training extends the box-size distribution while retaining throw, dynamics, contact, and recovery randomization. Stage 2 samples object-observation latency once per episode from one to three control steps (2060 ms), training the controller to act on delayed perception; the camera-to-control latency of our detector-based hardware pipeline (69 ms median; Tab. IV) exceeds this range, and Stage 3 targets add further 40 ms lag. In single-seed comparison, controller trained without it is 511 points lower at every tested delay (Sec. V-D). Figure 3 illustrates the variations; numerical settings are given in Sec. V-A. The resulting encoder and decoder are frozen for Stage 3. C. Appearance thus reaches the GRU only through the localization heatmap; in simulation, ego-motion comes from the simulator. Two output heads predict the dynamics latent and auxiliary position/velocity; the latter supplies training supervision, while only the latent drives the decoder. b) Two-step visual training: The Stage 2 privileged encoder Eφ and action decoder πθ stay fixed throughout visual training. We train the visual encoder in two steps. First, we train the RGB-D CNN and box-localization heatmap using Gaussian targets at projected box centers with binary cross-entropy supervision. The nonnegative weights α j, normalized to average one, reflect the fixed decoders action sensitivity to one-standard-deviation latent errors. The coefficient λaux balances auxiliary supervision, and ωt emphasizes close-range observations (Sec. V-A). c) Visual-policy data aggregation: Initial data come from privileged-controller rollouts. We then run the visual controller, label its visited states with the fixed privileged encoder, aggregate the data, and refit the GRU and output heads with the localizer and controller fixed. This second DAgger-style procedure [32] provides latent targets for the views encountered under visual control. Unlike the actionlabeled aggregation in Stage 2, it supervises the predicted latent rather than the controllers action. Cached geometric features, ego-motion, and privileged observations provide aligned sequences and latent labels. Windows stay within episodes; validation uses separate episodes, and aggregation-round selection and final evaluation use separate throws. d) Appearance adaptation: We augment box colors during localizer pretraining and rollout collection; localizer pretraining also applies random RGB gain and offset, pixel noise, small image shifts, and about 2.4 cm depth noise, and the temporal model is fit on noise-perturbed features with the color-augmented localizer frozen. Motion blur, auto-exposure dynamics, and structured depth artifacts are not modeled. D. Downstream Carrying and Handover The downstream demonstration in Fig. 1 connects the catching policy to the pretrained SONIC motion controller [22] for walking with the retained box and handover. Visual human detection identifies the recipient for the handover stage. supervisor transfers command authority after persistent near-chest box evidence and low leg velocity, torso tilt, and base speed establish settled hold. Hold-state persistence accommodates close-range occlusion. At transfer, the supervisor establishes the navigation frame and switches gains and observations to SONIC. The reference holds the current posture for 2 before transitioning to standing cradle for walking and handover. MuJoCo deployment twin checks perception, communication, joint commands, and controller transfer. In the 20-trial downstream task evaluation, cumulative success rates are 65% after catching, 35% after carrying, 30% after handover, and 25% after return. V. EXPERIMENTS Our experiments address four questions: Q1: How well does Reflex catch in simulation and on the real robot, compared with privileged input and human catchers? Q2: How do the catching objective and motion priors shape whole-body control, and how does catching vary with box size and payload? Q3: How should the object-dynamics latent be learned, and how does it handle lateral offsets and perception delay? Q4: Which visual inputs and supervision ground the latent in egocentric vision, and how do appearance, distance, and detector-based perception affect it? In the tables, pink identifies proposed configurations, gray denotes references or auxiliary diagnostic rates, and bold marks the highest catch rate in each comparison, excluding gray references. The abbreviation w/o means without, and GT denotes ground truth. A. Experimental Setup a) Training settings: Stage 1 uses randomized state observations; its teacher is queried with ground-truth box position and velocity, and the ground-truth reference feeds ideal box measurements through its Kalman filter. Stage 2 BC initialization uses five data-aggregation rounds and gives visible-box samples fivefold weight. Stage 2 joint PPO uses 4096 environments, 600 iterations, and an initial learning rate of 104, without additional latent noise or wholevector dropout. Release distances span 2.55.0 m; box size is randomized among three sizes: 251913, 342622, and 423227 cm. The privileged encoder has two 64-unit residual hidden layers. The visual model combines eight geometric features and nine ego-motion features using two-layer, 128-unit GRU. The color-augmented localizer is pretrained for 20 epochs with batch size 32 and learning rate 3104. Temporal training uses AdamW for 60 epochs with batch size 512 and maximum learning rate 2 103. Sequence training uses λaux = 0.5 and an eightfold sample weight at box ranges of 0.52.5 m, normalized within each minibatch. Visual training uses two or three DAgger rounds per controller, selected on held-out evaluation throws. On one RTX 3090, renderingfree Stage 2 PPO runs at about 28k environment steps/s (4096 environments), whereas rendering 192 144 RGB-D in the loop runs at about 1.5k steps/s (320 environments): the 59M steps of Stage 2 PPO take about 35 min instead of roughly 11 h, while Stage 3 renders about 1.6M steps. b) Evaluation protocol and comparisons: Each environment contributes one throw from 3.03.5 with 34 26 22 cm box. Evaluation starts without held box, scores from the first step, and ends after 640 steps before reset. Rethrows, deliberately unreachable targets, robot pushes, and held-box kicks are disabled. Reference start frames are uniformly sampled from the standing segment, independently of the policy. Throw attitude, spin, aim scatter, physical properties, and reset-state noise remain randomized. catch requires chestregion support, wrists flanking the box, clearance from head/shoulder support, and low box speed for 0.6 s. Torso excursion records whether tilt reaches 38 between launch and evaluation end, separately from catch success and falls. The initialization comparison trains six controllers per latent configuration and evaluates each on 640 held-out throws (3840 throws per configuration); the controllers share the predecessor policy and, for our configuration, BC initialization. Tables report mean catch rates. The state-policy reference uses one checkpoint. Both inherit the decoder body and use the same architecture and control interface. Ours uses BC initialization; the state-initialized alternative aligns encoder coordinates with position/velocity and maps the predecessors input weights without BC. Both continue joint encoder/decoder PPO training (Tab. VII). Because box geometry changes, the size columns instead require the box to settle within 0.65 of the pelvis below 1.2 m/s for 0.6 s, stay above 0.35 m, and remain at rest at 12.8 s; early resets fail. Interception requires the box to slow below 1 m/s near the torso, irrespective of retention. The visual-latent rows use the color-augmented visual component. B. Overall Performance For Q1 in simulation, the visual controller catches 3290/3840 throws (85.7%), compared with 87.9% using privileged latent input to the same decoder (Tab. VII), so visual prediction preserves most of the catch performance. On the real robot, Tab. II reports 20 trials per condition. Catch success reaches 65%, 40%, and 15% for the regular box at 2.5, 5, and 7 and ranges from 30% to 60% across the tested payloads; with 20 trials, 95% Wilson intervals span up to about 20 points. As human reference, three people each caught 20 regular-box throws per distance, standing with arms relaxed until release. Pooled human success is 85.0%, 68.3%, and 28.3% at 2.5, 5, and 7 m; the real G1 reaches 76% and 59% of it at 2.5 and 5 (95% intervals 54107% and 33103%), and both are low at 7 m, which approaches the practical range of human throwing and catching. C. Whole-Body Control To answer Q2, we ablate the Stage 1 objective, reused in latent PPO, and examine box size and payload. a) Reward objective: Rewards are removed only during Stage 2 PPO from the shared initialization, so Tab. III tests what retains and extends the skill. PPO raises success from 75.3% to 88.6% for centered throws and from 44.2% to 76.1% at 0.6 offset. Removing hold shaping reduces offset success to 50.8%; removing all three task groups gives 2.7%. Removing tracking or AMP alone costs 45 points, not significant over three seeds; removing both collapses training (a foot-height termination ends most episodes), and no episode reaches the throw. One checkpoint catches 91.7% but has 72% excursion; another catches 86.2% with 1% excursion. These post-launch metrics distinguish successful box retention from settled whole-body posture. Ridge probes with quadratic features on held-out flight ticks decode the delayed box position and velocity from (R2 0.940.99 and 0.900.99 across the six controllers) but not box size, orientation, or angular velocity (R2 0.13), whereas the weight-mapped latent keeps position and velocity linearly (R2 0.98) and retains some orientation (R2 up to 0.58). probe of the boxs current, undelayed state (first controller of each configuration) shows that partly compensates for observation age: for samples at least 80 ms old, it predicts the current position and velocity with RMSE 0.33 and 1.5 m/s, against 0.6 0.7 and 3.4 m/s for the delayed sample itself and 0.40 and 2.1 m/s for the weight-mapped latent, which stays closer to the delayed observation. trained without latency randomization (one training seed each), which is 511 points lower at every delay; beyond the training range, both decline (32.3% and 27.0% at 120 ms). The 60 and 80 ms columns bracket the 69 ms median of our detector-based hardware pipeline, so the zero-delay rates elsewhere are likely optimistic for hardware. With privileged input at matched total delay (added delay plus the 40 ms label lag), success falls from 88.3% at 40 ms to 76.4% at 120 ms, against 88.4% to 60.9% with visual input, so most of the visual decline arises in the encoder, whose training inputs are not delayed. The latency-randomized controller is most successful at 60 ms of delay (91.9% vs. 82.7% without delay; privileged input), whereas the one trained without delay peaks at zero (84.5%), consistent with the controller compensating for the latency it was trained with. Across seven tested colors, During latent PPO, retaining the catching skill requires the task rewards, chiefly hold shaping, and at least one motion prior; payloads up to 2 kg remain catchable, whereas boxes outside the reference size are often intercepted but not retained, and torso excursion separates retention from settled posture. For object dynamics, BC initialization improves visual catching by 5.2 points on average, and in single-seed comparison, latency randomization adds 511 points across simulated delays. For visual grounding, temporal history and ego-motion contribute most, regressing the learned latent gives higher success than the evaluated full-state regression baseline, and, with the same detector, the learned latent outperforms detection plus Kalman filtering within its visual training range and, once Stage 3 data cover them, also on 5 and 7 throws. The main limitation is long-range visual grounding: on 5 throws, faster than any training throw and beyond the 3.03.5 Stage 3 data, visual success falls to 43.0% while privileged input reaches 79.7%, and real-robot success falls to 40% and 15% at 5 and 7 m; adding far throws to the Stage 3 data raises simulated 5 success to 75.8%, not yet tested on hardware. Further limitations: single task with human throws and 20 real trials per condition (intervals up to about 20 points); hardware latency was measured only on our detector-based pipeline, where it exceeds the randomized range; the controller is effectively size-blind; and rendering omits motion blur and exposure dynamics. VII. CONCLUSION Reflex learns visual reactive whole-body catching on humanoid by decoupling whole-body control, object dynamics, and visual grounding into three stages linked by an object-dynamics latent. In simulation, visual control reaches 85.7% catch success versus 87.9% with privileged input, and on real Unitree G1 it catches human-thrown boxes at 76% and 59% of human success at 2.5 and 5 m. Extending this decomposition to other visual reactive whole-body tasks is natural next step. success is 87.088.9% in this evaluation run (86.687.8% on six colors in the separate run of Tab. I), demonstrating reduced appearance sensitivity. c) Learned latent versus detection plus filtering: The visual gap grows with throw distance: at 5 m, privileged latent input matches the state policy (79.7%), whereas visual input reaches 43.0%, although the encoder still detects the box on every 5 and 7 throw. For like-for-like comparison with detection plus filtering, two baselines use our own color-augmented heatmap CNN (same rendered training data, camera, and resolution) and pass its per-frame 3D box point to Kalman filter with gravity and drag whose speed bound, noise, gating, and output lag are selected on held-out throws; both receive ground-truth arm trigger, which raises the arms earlier than ours. The filtered state drives either the state policy (Detector (our CNN) + state-based in Tab. I) or, encoded by Eφ , our decoder (Detector (our CNN) + latent decoder), which isolates the learned temporal model. Excluding the 5 and 7 throws, which lie beyond the Stage 3 data, the visual latent outperforms the state-based pipeline in all 13 conditions of Tab. (by 5.015.6 points) and the latent-decoder pipeline in 14 of 18 conditions of Tab. and Fig. 4 (mean +1.5 points, largest for box size; with the same trigger, 88.3 vs. 84.5% at the reference and 69.8 vs. 65.2% at 0.6 m; across five further controllers at 0 and 0.6 the margin is +0.3 5.2 points, ahead in 7 of 10 cells), so its advantage over detection plus filtering comes from the Stage 2 latent interface, while the learned filter is on par with tuned Kalman filter. At 5 and 7 the filtered pipelines catch more (67.7 and 33.9% for the latent decoder), but this reflects the Stage 3 data range: adding 2.57 throws to Stage 3 raises visual success to 75.8 and 36.7%, with 88.8% at the reference. The Detector (YOLO) row reproduces our previously deployed perception node (real-photo weights, hardware depth and size checks, untuned filter) and serves only as reference. F. Real-Robot Evaluation To test the conditions of Q2Q4 on hardware, we evaluate catches of human-thrown boxes with different sizes, payloads, throw distances, and lateral offsets. Unless the size is varied, real-robot trials use the 31 26 21 cm regular box. Figure 5 shows qualitative catches across these conditions. Human throwers cannot place the box at precise lateral offset; of 20 throws aimed to either side (e.g., 0.9 right and 0.7 left in Fig. 5), the G1 caught 8. a) Hardware runtime: Tab. IV reports measurements from two hardware sessions of our detector-based pipeline (1274 box measurements and approximately 33,000 control ticks). The 95th-percentile camera-to-control latency is 90.2 ms, and the 50 Hz control period exceeds 25 ms on 0.015% of ticks. VI. DISCUSSION AND LIMITATIONS The decomposition lets visual grounding be learned with the controller fixed and keeps rendering out of reinforcement learning, so only about 1.6M rendered steps are needed.
